description_ru: Брат и сестра впервые говорят о том, что делать с домом покойной матери, и решают разобрать его вместе.
text:
Claire: Thanks for coming, Mark. I know it's a long drive from Bristol.
Mark: It's only two hours. Besides, you said it was important. What's going on? You sounded strange on the phone.
Claire: Come in and sit down. Tea? I've got the good biscuits.
Mark: The good biscuits. Now I'm worried.
Claire: Don't be silly. It's about the house. Mum's house.
Mark: Ah. I wondered whether we would finally talk about that.
Claire: I think we have to. Six months have passed since the funeral, and we've done nothing except pay the electricity bill.

Mark: I know. Every time I think about it, I get this heavy feeling in my stomach. I walked past it last month and couldn't even go in.
Claire: I went in last weekend. I wanted to tidy up the kitchen.
Mark: And?
Claire: I stood in the doorway for an hour and cried. Then I put the kettle on, because that's what she always did, and it was just the same smell. Toast and lavender.
Mark: Oh, Claire. I'm sorry. I should have gone with you.
Claire: It's not your fault. I wanted to go alone. But I made a decision, standing there with the kettle.
Mark: Which was?
Claire: I think we should sell it.

Mark: Sell it? Already?
Claire: Not tomorrow. But soon. The roof needs repairing, the garden has become a jungle, and nobody lives there. A house that's empty doesn't stay a home. It just becomes an expensive box.
Mark: But it's Mum's house. We grew up there. Dad planted the apple tree. I still know which stair squeaks.
Claire: The fourth one. I know, I know. Do you think I want to do this? It makes me feel like I'm selling her.
Mark: Then why do it?
Claire: Because I can't afford to pay for two houses. And you can't either.
Mark: I can manage for a while.
Claire: Can you? You told me last month you're thinking of leaving your job.

Mark: That's... different. And I only said I was thinking.
Claire: I'm not trying to start a fight. I only mean that money isn't the real issue, is it? We're afraid that if we sell the house, we'll lose her all over again.
Mark: Maybe. I hadn't thought of it that way. But then what's the solution? Keep it forever, like a museum?
Claire: No. I'd like us to go there together, one weekend. We take out everything that matters to us, we give the rest to charity, and then we decide properly.
Mark: Together. With no pressure.
Claire: With sandwiches, and the radio on, the way Mum used to do when she cleaned.
Mark: She sang along to everything, even the news.
Claire: And always out of tune.

Mark: Fine. I'll do it. But I have one condition.
Claire: Go on.
Mark: If we find the letters in her wardrobe, we read them together. No peeking by yourself.
Claire: What letters?
Mark: Don't pretend you don't know. She kept a shoebox in the top of her wardrobe. She told me when I was twelve that it was "private, forever".
Claire: A shoebox! I forgot all about it. I was fourteen, and I tried to open it once, and she caught me.
Mark: She told Dad you were practising to be a burglar.
Claire: And he laughed so much he dropped the shopping.

Claire: So, the weekend after next? I've already asked my boss for Friday.
Mark: You asked your boss before you asked me?
Claire: I knew you'd say yes in the end. I just wanted to save time.
Mark: That's very you. Always three steps ahead.
Claire: Somebody had to be. Someone has to remember the bills.
Mark: And somebody has to remember which stair squeaks. I'll bring a toolbox, in case we need to fix the roof.
Claire: You can't fix a roof, Mark. Last year you couldn't fix a shelf.
Mark: That shelf was crooked from the start. And I was in a hurry.

Claire: Do you want to know what scares me most?
Mark: Tell me.
Claire: That we'll find something in the house that we don't know about. Some part of her life that we never saw.
Mark: I've thought about that too. Maybe that's what the shoebox is.
Claire: Maybe. But she was our mother. Even if there are surprises, they can't change who she was.
Mark: No. They can only make her bigger. I think I'd like that.
Claire: Me too. Right. I'll book the cleaning bags and the skip, and you bring the toolbox that you can't use.
Mark: Deal. And Claire?
Claire: Yes?
Mark: Thanks for the biscuits. And for not doing it alone.

Claire: Don't mention it. Now eat another one, or I'll do it myself. They're Mum's favourite.
Mark: I know. I recognised them as soon as you opened the tin. Shortbread, with the little lemon stripe.
Claire: I bought six packets on Saturday. I couldn't stop.
Mark: Then we'd better start on the second packet.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Долгий звук между «э» и «ё», губы расслаблены; не произносите «р» в британском варианте.
Долгий «у», губы вытянуты вперёд; тяните звук.
Задняя часть языка опущена, кончик языка касается дёсен; не смягчайте «l» как русское «ль».
Кончик языка слегка между зубами, воздух выдыхайте мягко; не заменяйте на «с» или «з».

questions.question: Why did Claire ask Mark to come?
questions.answer: To talk about selling their late mother's house.

questions.question: What does Claire suggest they do first?
questions.answer: Go to the house together, keep what matters and give the rest to charity.

questions.question: What is Mark's condition?
questions.answer: They read any letters in the shoebox together.

questions.question: What does Claire fear most?
questions.answer: Finding something they never knew about their mother's life.
